newsitem.title: UK: ED&F Man sees 36,000 T cocoa surplus in 95/96.
newsitem.headline: ED&F Man sees 36,000 T cocoa surplus in 95/96.

text.p: Commodity traders ED&F Man projected on Thursday a world cocoa surplus of 36,000 tonnes in the current 1995/96 (Oct/Sept) season, up from its May forecast of a 2,000-tonne surplus.
In its September cocoa report, Man Cocoa saw total Ivory Coast output at a record of 1.125 million tonnes, up from its previous forecast of 1.10 million and against 1994/95's harvest of 876,000.
The UK firm said cocoa could return to a supply deficit in the coming 1996/97 harvest due to anticipated significantly lower West African and Brazilian crops.
The last time cocoa was in deficit was in 1994/95, when it recorded a gap of 200,000 tonnes.
But Man gave no figures and a company official said its assessment of the world's 1996/97 supply/demand balance would only be published in its next crop report due in January.
There was market talk earlier in the week that Man could report a supply shortfall of between 150,000 and 180,000 tonnes for the coming season.
A host of crop data released over the past few days by other forecasters put the deficit at between 150,000 and 225,000 tonnes.
The Man report put the Ghanaian 1995/96 crop at the highest for 20 years at 390,000 tonnes compared with its previous forecast of 365,000 tonnes.
But the outlook in Malaysia had deteriorated further.
Man pegged Malaysian output at 105,000 tonnes, down from its previous forecast of 120,000, due to the country's low bean and product exports.
Man forecast the total 1995/96 world net cocoa harvest at a record 2.732 million tonnes against 1994/95's 2.344 million.
The gross harvest (before deducting one percent for loss in weight) was seen at 2.760 million tonnes against 2.368 million.
Total world grindings were seen at 2.697 million tonnes against 2.544 million in 1994/95.
It put the ratio of end-season stocks to world consumption at 40.6 percent by the end of the 1995/96 season against 41.7 percent a year earlier.
Man said grindings in the five largest processing nations rose over 12 percent in the second quarter of 1996.
"We estimate that grindings will increase by six percent this season, the highest growth rate since 1988/89," it said.
"Chocolate consumption growth has been strong in 1996, even in the more mature markets of Western Europe and North America."
